articles.title: Offline reverse geocoding on iPhone with one memory-mapped file
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I work on ClearWhirl, an iPhone app that works out what is in your photo library on the device, with no upload. Places is one of its features. Every photo with a location carries a latitud…
articles.body: Disclosure: I work on ClearWhirl, an iPhone app that works out what is in your photo library on the device, with no upload. Places is one of its features. Every photo with a location carries a latitude and longitude. Turning that into "Lisbon, Portugal" normally means CLGeocoder , which sends the coordinates to Apple's servers and is rate limited. For an app whose promise is that your library never leaves the phone, and which has to do it for thousands of photos, that was a non-starter. We replaced it with one bundled binary file, memory-mapped, and plain geometry. This is how it works. What reading the location costs you PHAsset.location is metadata. No new permission is needed beyond the photo library access you already have, and no pixel is read.
articles.author: appi korn

articles.title: The Hopper Trap: When the Optimal Tile Size Wastes Half Your Register File
articles.excerpt: TL;DR On NVIDIA Hopper, a larger tile can create enough register pressure to make a "smaller" configuration ~30% faster. In a December 2023 Colfax Research case study implementing FlashAttention-2, th…
articles.body: TL;DR On NVIDIA Hopper, a larger tile can create enough register pressure to make a "smaller" configuration ~30% faster. In a December 2023 Colfax Research case study implementing FlashAttention-2, the supposedly optimal 128×128 tile hit 208.7 TFLOPs/s, while 128×64 hit 295.7 TFLOPs/s. The fix was counterintuitive: deliberately leave register capacity unused. This post walks through why. The performance paradox When optimizing GPU kernels, bigger tiles seem like the obvious choice: more data per tile, better reuse, fewer iterations, higher throughput. A December 2023 Colfax Research case study implementing FlashAttention-2 on Hopper benchmarked different tile configurations.
articles.author: Dikhyant Krishna Dalai

articles.excerpt: If your team writes ASP.NET Core and is about to build something in TypeScript (a service next to a frontend that's already in TypeScript, a backend for a product that's leaving .NET, or just a team t…
articles.body: If your team writes ASP.NET Core and is about to build something in TypeScript (a service next to a frontend that's already in TypeScript, a backend for a product that's leaving .NET, or just a team that wants one language), the Node.js world can look like a pile of small libraries you're expected to assemble yourself. Express, a validation library, a DI container someone picked, a folder structure someone invented. Coming from a framework where dotnet new webapi gives you DI, configuration, logging, validation and a request pipeline out of the box, that's a step back, and it's a fair objection. Nest is the framework that takes those decisions for you.

articles.title: Argo CD vs Flux: choosing a GitOps tool for AWS EKS
articles.excerpt: Both Argo CD and Flux are CNCF-graduated GitOps controllers that pull the desired state of your Kubernetes clusters from Git and keep the clusters in line with it. They solve the same problem and both…
articles.body: Both Argo CD and Flux are CNCF-graduated GitOps controllers that pull the desired state of your Kubernetes clusters from Git and keep the clusters in line with it. They solve the same problem and both are production-grade; the difference is in how they model applications, how much they put in front of your developers, and how they fit a multi-team platform. Short version: Argo CD gives you an application-centric model with a first-party UI, SSO and RBAC out of the box — the better default when many teams will deploy through it and need to see what is happening. Flux is a set of composable controllers that feel like native Kubernetes resources — the better default for platform teams that want GitOps as infrastructure plumbing, with image automation built in and no UI to run.

articles.title: One flood-fill for both the preview and the turn in a browser puzzle
articles.excerpt: When a grid puzzle previews a move, players use that preview to make a decision. If a shelter looks dry after placing a barrier, it should stay dry when the turn runs. Jade Canal, a 5×5 puzzle from Hu…
articles.body: When a grid puzzle previews a move, players use that preview to make a decision. If a shelter looks dry after placing a barrier, it should stay dry when the turn runs. Jade Canal, a 5×5 puzzle from Hundred-Realm Tower Defense, uses a single bounded flood-fill for both jobs. Model the tide as a distance limit Each surge supplies several inlets and a maximum reach. Start a breadth-first traversal with all the inlets at distance zero. From each cell, visit its orthogonal land neighbors and skip rocks, barriers, and cells already visited. Stop expanding a cell once it reaches the distance limit. Mark each cell as visited when you enqueue it so two inlets can converge without queuing the same cell twice.

articles.excerpt: App lock needs more than a Play system update.
articles.body: TL;DR Google has confirmed that Android’s native app lock cannot be backported to older Android versions via Play System updates. The current implementation depends on new APIs in the core Android platform. Users will need an Android OS update, not a Google Play System update, to get Google’s current implementation of App Lock. Between Samsung introducing native app lock in One UI 9.5 this week and Google restoring the feature in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 3 last month, it’s been a good few weeks for Android users who value their privacy. And with Google increasingly delivering Android features outside of major OS updates , some users are wondering whether their phones could get native app locking without upgrading to the latest version of Android.

articles.title: 53 Years Later, The Greatest Closing Line In Sci-Fi History Is Still The Best Book Quote Of The 1970s
articles.excerpt: Roadside Picnic ends with one of science fiction’s most beautiful lines, a simple wish for happiness that still resonates more than 50 years later.
articles.body: The canon of science-fiction literature is home to countless unforgettable endings, from 1984 ’s short but devastating retrospective ("He loved Big Brother") to The Three-Body Problem ’s defiant reminder that humanity cannot be so easily wiped out. The best sci-fi endings don't offer comfortable closure. Instead, they reframe everything that came before. In their closing lines, great sci-fi novelists leave readers suspended in the aftermath, forced to stew in the terrifying logic of cold technology, the fragility of human nature, and the vast expanse of space.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

articles.body: A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage. The company notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms. You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar. But on Tuesday (Nov. 17), SpaceX released up-close views — a series of four slo-mo videos captured by cameras near the top of the 480-foot-tall (146 meters) tower.
